Article Title: ‘Proud to be a dimagi naxal’: P Chidambaram hits back at PM Modi
Article Text:
File photo: PM Modi and senior Congress leader P Chidambaram

Congress attacks PM Modi’s ‘dimagi naxal’ remark

PM Modi says armed Naxalism ‘breathing its last’

NEW DELHI: Former Union minister and senior Congress leader P Chidambaram on Sunday hit back at Prime Minister Narendra Modi over his “dimagi naxal” remarks, saying he was “proud” to be described by the term.“I am proud to be a dimagi naxal!” Chidambaram said in a post on X, a day after PM Modi, in his 80th Independence Day address from the Red Fort, warned that although armed Naxalism was nearing its end, people with an ideological Naxal mindset continued to pose a threat.PM Modi had urged people to “identify and isolate” such individuals, saying they were looking for opportunities to promote violence and unrest and “drag the country on the wrong path”.The Prime Minister said his government had made ending Naxalism a priority after coming to power in 2014. He said decades of Maoist violence had destroyed the lives and aspirations of young people and claimed that more than 3,500 security personnel had been killed in the conflict.“Naxalism, Maoism destroyed the dreams of lakhs of youth. It stole the sons of numerous mothers, crushed the dreams of numerous mothers,” PM Modi said in his Independence Day address.He also alleged that people with a Maoist mindset had earlier occupied positions of influence in government committees and policymaking.“For years, people with Maoist thinking were there in public life, even in government committees this thinking had affected various institutions and initiatives,” PM Modi said, before calling for the “dimagi naxal” to be identified and isolated.Chidambaram's response came a day after Congress had already attacked PM Modi over the remarks.Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh accused the Prime Minister of reviving the “urban naxal” label to target political opponents. He argued that the government had previously used the term despite Union home minister Amit Shah clarifying in Parliament that there was no official definition of “urban Naxal”.Ramesh also alleged that the government eventually adopted some of the issues raised by people it had labelled “urban Naxals”. He cited the caste census as an example, saying the idea had earlier been dismissed as reflecting “urban Naxal” thinking before the government announced a caste-based census.“First, you make derogatory remarks--calling them 'Urban Naxals' or 'Mental Naxals'--but later, you accept the very demands your political opponents were making,” Ramesh said, according to news agency ANI.The Congress leader had also earlier called PM Modi a “master abuser” in “Entire Political Science” while reacting to his use of the “urban naxal” and “dimagi naxal” labels.The broader Opposition has also criticised PM Modi's remarks. CPI(M) general secretary M A Baby said his party opposed Naxalism but accused the government of using the “Naxal mentality” label to target political opponents.CPI general secretary D Raja described “dimagi naxal” as an attempt to stigmatise dissent.TMC leader Saket Gokhale similarly accused PM Modi of using the Independence Day platform to take “cheap shots” at his critics.PM Modi's remarks came as he declared that the government had made substantial progress in tackling armed Naxalism.He said Naxalism had kept large parts of the country and its population “hostage” for decades and had resulted in the deaths of thousands of security personnel.“In 2014, when you gave us the opportunity we had decided that we will rid the country of naxalism, and today I am happy to announce that naxalism does not have even the strength for breathing,” PM Modi said.At the same time, he cautioned that the end of armed insurgency did not mean the ideological challenge had disappeared.“Even if these naxals are gone, but the 'dimagi naxal' (people with naxal thinking), are looking for an opportunity, looking to see ways of violence, and trying to drag the country to a wrong path,” PM Modi said.He linked the issue to his broader call for young people to contribute to the government's vision of a developed India by 2047, arguing that remote areas once affected by Naxal violence were now seeing development.
Article Summary: Former Union minister P Chidambaram hits back at PM Modi over 'dimagi naxal' remarks. PM Modi had warned that armed Naxalism was nearing its end. He had urged people to 'identify and isolate' such individuals. Congress has accused PM Modi of using the term to target political opponents.

Article Title: 3 injured in NIS Patiala ceiling collapse
Article Text: Patiala: The false ceiling of a hall at Netaji Subhas National Institute of Sports (NIS) in Patiala, a top centre of Sports Authority of India, collapsed during an Independence Day function on Saturday, injuring three students, reports Bharat Khanna.Videos of the cave-in show members of the audience scrambling to safety."No one sustained any major injury. The safety...of athletes, trainees, staff and visitors at NIS remain the institution's highest priority," NIS director Sumit Miglani said. Civil Lines SHO said no one had filed any police complaint. NIS, housed in the erstwhile palace of Patiala Maharaja, has produced generations of national coaches and athletes.
Article Summary: False ceiling of a hall at Netaji Subhas National Institute of Sports collapsed during an Independence Day function on Saturday. Three students were injured. NIS, housed in the erstwhile palace of Patiala Maharaja, has produced generations of national coaches and athletes.

Article Title: Harsimrat Kaur Badal 'deeply touched' by PM Modi's 'kind gesture' after attack on Sukhbir Badal
Article Text:
Sukhbir Badal was attacked at a gurudwara in Maharashtra's Nanded

NEW DELHI: Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) MP Harsimrat Kaur Badal on Friday said she was “deeply touched” by Prime Minister Narendra Modi ’s “kind gesture” of reaching out to enquire about the health of her husband and party chief, Sukhbir Singh Badal , who was attacked at a gurdwara in Maharashtra’s Nanded a day earlier.This marked the Badal family's first reaction to the attack on the former Punjab deputy chief minister."Truly grateful, Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri @narendramodi ji, for your personal call to inquire about Sardar Sukhbir Singh Badal ji’s health and for your good wishes for his speedy recovery following the dastardly attack on him inside a Gurudwara Sahib in Nanded, Maharashtra," Harsimrat Badal, SAD's only Lok Sabha MP, wrote on X.She also thanked the prime minister for taking immediate cognisance of the incident and directing central investigating agencies to coordinate with the state police in the probe."Your concern, support and wishes during this difficult time mean a lot to all of us in the family, our party and to the people of Punjab. I am deeply touched by your kind gesture. I am also grateful to you for taking immediate cognisance of the incident and directing central investigating agencies to coordinate with Maharashtra Police in the probe," the Bathinda MP added.On Thursday, Sukhbir Singh Badal was injured after being attacked by a kirpan-wielding assailant while leaving the Mata Sahib Devaji Gurdwara at Mudkhed in Maharashtra’s Nanded district. The assailant was arrested at the spot.Maharashtra chief minister Devendra Fadnavis ordered an inquiry into the attack and spoke to Sukhbir Singh Badal over the phone. The SAD president is learnt to have told Fadnavis that he was stable, ANI reported.Earlier, Badal was also targeted in an attempted shooting at the Golden Temple in Amritsar in December 2024 while he was performing “seva”. The attacker allegedly tried to fire at him but was overpowered before he could cause any harm.The 2024 attack took place while Badal was carrying out “seva” after the Akal Takht, the highest temporal authority in Sikhism, declared him a “tankhaiya,” or guilty of religious misconduct, over decisions taken by the SAD-led Punjab government between 2007 and 2017.The SAD and BJP, which currently lead the governments at the Centre and in Maharashtra, are former allies. In 2020, the SAD ended its alliance with the BJP in protest against the Centre’s contentious farm laws, which were later withdrawn.Sukhbir Singh Badal met Prime Minister Narendra Modi last week, triggering speculation that the former allies could reunite ahead of the Punjab assembly elections early next year.
Article Summary: Harsimrat Kaur Badal said she was “deeply touched” by Prime Minister Narendra Modi ’s “kind gesture” of reaching out to enquire about the health of her husband and party chief. Sukhbir Singh Badal was attacked at a gurdwara in Maharashtra’s Nanded a day earlier.

Article Title: 'Go after the terrorists wherever they are': Ajit Doval reveals PM Modi's brief on Op Sindoor
Article Text:
Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: National security adviser Ajit Doval offered a rare glimpse into the strategic thinking behind Op Sindoor, revealing for the first time in detail how India set its objectives for the 88-hour military operation launched in response to the Pahalgam terror attack and set out to destroy the terrorist infrastructure responsible for it, reports Rajshekhar Jha.Recalling the tense atmosphere following the Pahalgam massacre, Doval detailed PM Modi’s immediate reaction on cutting short his foreign visit. “At the airport itself, we had a meeting. First, he wanted to know all the facts. And then his first question to me was, who has done it,” Doval said.“We will go after them. Zameen mein ho, aasman mein ho, paatal mein ho, woh log jahan bhi hai... We will not forgive them,” Doval quoted Modi as saying."Thanks to our intelligence agencies... they did a brilliant job and within a short period of time, we were able to identify the perpetrators and act with precision," Ajit Doval said.The national security adviser, widely seen as one of the architects of the retaliation for the Pahalgam attack, indicated that India had made up its mind to go to any extent."Once it starts, we are willing to go as far as necessary for a nation to preserve its sovereignty and...thereare no limits on that. We fight till the last drop of blood. India's being more tolerant should not be mistaken for its weakness," Doval said, confirming that the terrorists who had targeted their victims on the basis of faith had breached the country's pain threshold.The perpetrators had audaciously taunted the Indian leadership, daring it to retaliate. "They (Pahalgam terrorists) had told victims that 'jaake Modi ko bol do jo kar sakta hai kar le'," the NSA recalled.Doval said India had decided at the outset that the operation would focus on destroying enemy camps associated with the Pahalgam attack, which took place on April 22, 2025, claiming the lives of 26 innocent people."We wanted the Pakistan Army to realise that this support to terrorism or inability to take effective action against the terrorists is something which is not tolerable to us... Basically, the world is very clear: India's generosity or India's being more tolerant should not be mistaken for its weakness," he said.The NSA described Operation Sindoor as evidence of India's growing technological and military capabilities.
Article Summary: National security adviser Ajit Doval offers rare glimpse into the strategic thinking behind Op Sindoor. Reveals for the first time in detail how India set its objectives for the 88-hour military operation launched in response to the Pahalgam terror attack.

Article Title: Full Vande Mataram rendition triggers fresh Congress-BJP clash
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: A political row erupted after a video from the Independence Day programme at Congress headquarters showed Congress Parliamentary Party (CCP) chairperson Sonia Gandhi gesturing and engaged in an exchange of comments with party president Mallikarjun Kharge , drawing the attention of others, including Rahul Gandhi, who was standing at some distance.BJP MP Anurag Thakur said Sonia, Rahul and Kharge looked "uneasy" as 'Vande mataram's' full version was rendered. "Congress, due to its petty and appeasement politics, has insulted the national song," said the former minister."Kharge Ji is said to be party chief, but Sonia Gandhi, by shouting and angrily gesticulating, has shown the world who is the real boss. This is the reality of their belief in Dalit empowerment," said Thakur, referring to the Congress president's caste background.However, Congress MP Jairam Ramesh said: "As the Congress president was standing for a long time, Sonia ji was asking for a chair for him." He added the song's full version was played.Anurag said that since the days of Nehru, Congress has been opposed to the full version and confined its singing to the first two paras. This was reflected in what happened at the Congress headquarters, he added.Ramesh recalled that on Oct 28, 1937, a meeting of the Congress Working Committee was held in Calcutta in the presence of Gandhi, Bose, Sardar Patel, Maulana Abul Kalam Azad, Nehru, GB Pant and C Rajagopalachari, and at the advice of Tagore, they decided that the initial stanzas of Vande would be sung at Congress sessions. "We have been singing those lines in every session since then," he added.Rendition of 'Vande Mataram' at Congress sessions was restricted to the first two stanzas following objections from Muslims who said the song is idolatrous and against their religious beliefs.
Article Summary: Video shows Sonia Gandhi gesturing and engaged in an exchange of comments with party president Mallikarjun Kharge. BJP MP Anurag Thakur said Sonia, Rahul and Kharge looked "uneasy" as 'Vande mataram's' full version was rendered.

Article Title: Had Article 370 stayed, PoK may have sought to rejoin J&K: Omar Abdullah
Article Text:
Omar paid tribute to his grandfather and National Conference founder Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

SRINAGAR: J&K CM Omar Abdullah credited Kashmiris with fighting the 1947 tribal invasion before Indian troops arrived and said people across the LoC might have been protesting to rejoin J&K today had Centre not revoked Article 370 in 2019.Speaking at an Independence Day event Saturday, Omar paid tribute to his grandfather and National Conference founder Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah, portraying his role in resisting the Pakistan-backed tribal invasion as central to J&K’s history.“Before Indian Army reached here, it was the people of J&K who fought the tribal invaders, who fought the infiltrators sent from across, who fought the soldiers sent from across,” Omar said. “Thousands of brave people” sacrificed their lives, he said.Omar’s remarks came as his govt continues to press for restoration of J&K’s statehood, while Sheikh Abdullah’s legacy remains a political fault line after the abrogation of Article 370.Recent unrest in PoK sharpened Omar’s argument. “When I see the situation today across the LoC, I realise that the decision taken by our leaders 80 years ago for us was the right decision,” Omar said, underscoring Sheikh Abdullah preferring India’s secular ideals over Pakistan and supporting J&K’s accession in 1947.Pakistani security firing has killed dozens following protests demanding abolition of 12 seats in the 53-member PoK assembly reserved for refugees from J&K who settled there after 1947. Protesters say the seats let Pakistani parties wield influence in PoK.Omar said the condition of PoK made him wonder what might have happened had J&K’s situation not changed in 2019. “Perhaps… people of that part of J&K would be protesting to rejoin us today,” he said. “That part of J&K Kashmir is ours. We consider those people as our own. No one is a stranger. No one is an outsider.”Omar also made federalism a central plank of his speech. “Federalism suffers when central agencies start interfering in the affairs of the states,” he said. Restoring J&K’s statehood should be part of a broader effort to strengthen all states rather than federalism being reduced to “only words”, he added.Omar also criticised NEET and JEE, saying states had lost their right to conduct admissions to their medical and engineering colleges. National examinations made sense for national institutions such as IITs, IIMs and NIFT, but state institutions should retain the right to conduct exams and grant admissions, he said.
Article Summary: J&K CM Omar Abdullah credited Kashmiris with fighting the 1947 tribal invasion before Indian troops arrived. He said people across the LoC might have been protesting to rejoin J&K today had Centre not revoked Article 370 in 2019. Omar also criticised NEET and JEE, saying states had lost their right to conduct admissions to their medical and engineering colleges.

Article Title: Army dog Tsyon shot in leg by terrorists in Kishtwar gets President I-Day honour
Article Text:
Tyson is the only animal hero among the 89 personnel chosen for MiD, which is an official military commendation.

Tyson is part of the elite squad of Army assault dogs, which are trained like soldiers for high-risk operations.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: New Delhi: Indian Army’s assault dog Tyson, who is attached to 2 Para Special Forces, has been honoured during the Independence Day 2026 celebrations for showing “bravery and extraordinary courage” during a counter-insurgency operation in J&K as part of Operation Rakshak early this year.The name of Tyson, a German Shepherd of Remount Veterinary Corps, appeared among 89 Mention-in-Despatches (MiD) approved by President Droupadi Murmu on I-Day eve on Friday.Tyson is the only animal hero among the 89 personnel chosen for MiD, which is an official military commendation recognising bravery and meritorious service in a combat zone.During Operation Trashi-I in Chatroo belt of J&K’s Kishtwar district on Feb 22 this year, Tyson scouted ahead of the troops and located a hidden terrorist hideout.“Tyson displayed extraordinary courage by taking the first bullet while leading the entry into the terrorists’ hideout. Undeterred by his injuries, he pressed forward and launched a fierce assault, compelling the terrorists to open fire and thereby confirming their presence. His fearless action enabled troops of White Knight Corps, J&K police and CRPF to precisely engage and neutralise three Pakistan-sponsored terrorists,” Army had said in a post on X.Tyson was then airlifted to Command Hospital Udhampur for emergency treatment and has now recovered. “Wounded yet in high spirits, alert and recovering well, Tyson exemplifies unwavering devotion to duty, a true warrior and a soldier in every sense,” Army said later.Tyson is part of the elite squad of Army assault dogs, which are trained like soldiers for high-risk operations. They are used in a situation where a human soldier may be exposed to immediate danger, locating hidden terrorists, detecting threats and helping troops establish the enemy’s position.The honour formally acknowledges the frontline role military dogs play in counter-terror operations. Mention-in-Despatches recipients do not receive a gallantry medal, but they get an official certificate and the right to wear a specific emblem on the ribbon of their campaign medal.
Article Summary: Tyson is part of the elite squad of Army assault dogs, which are trained like soldiers for high-risk operations. He scouted ahead of the troops and located a hidden terrorist hideout. Tyson was airlifted to Command Hospital Udhampur for emergency treatment and has now recovered.

Article Title: 'Remove bulletproof glass or I won't speak': Ex-officer recalls PM Modi's demand on I-Day 2014
Article Text:
PM Modi said, 'if this stays in front of me, I would not be able to address the citizens'," the officer recalled.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Former defence secretary RK Mathur has recalled how Prime Minister Narendra Modi insisted on removing the bulletproof glass barrier from the Red Fort before delivering his first Independence Day address as Prime Minister in 2014.Speaking about the episode, Mathur said he and the then Director of the Intelligence Bureau (IB) had briefed Modi about the security arrangements ahead of August 15. The officials had specifically discussed the bulletproof glass barrier placed in front of the Prime Minister."Me and the Director of Intelligence Bureau (IB), went to PM Modi for a briefing before August 15 because it was his first Independence Day where he would address the country from the ramparts of the Red Fort (as the Prime Minister).""During that conversation we explained him (PM Modi) that there is a barrier in front of him which is the bulletproof glass. PM Modi said, 'if this stays in front of me, I would not be able to address the citizens'," he told news agency IANS.Mathur said security officials initially opposed removing the shield because of the risks involved. The location offers a wide view of the surrounding area, including buildings in Chandni Chowk, making security arrangements particularly sensitive."From our side, this was naturally a security issue. As people know, the entire Chandni Chowk area is visible from there (Red Fort) where there are many buildings. That is why, from a security standpoint we urged the Prime Minister to rethink his decision. However, PM Modi clearly stated that if this (bulletproof shield) is not removed, he will not address."The former defence secretary said the security team eventually agreed to Modi's demand and removed the glass barrier just hours before the Independence Day ceremony."Due to this, I and the director of IB changed our standpoint and decided to remove the bulletproof glass. This glass shield was then removed on the intervening night of August 14 and 15, at about 2 am," Mathur added.The episode was recalled as Modi once again departed from established security protocol during the 80th Independence Day celebrations on Saturday, when he met schoolchildren, NCC cadets and 'My Bharat' volunteers at the Red Fort after his address.During the interaction, a young girl approached Modi and bent down to touch his feet. As she did so, her cap slipped from her head and fell to the ground.Modi immediately bent down, picked up the cap and placed it back on the girl's head. The gesture drew smiles and applause from the children and people around them.
Article Summary: Former defence secretary RK Mathur has recalled how Prime Minister Narendra Modi insisted on removing the bulletproof glass barrier from the Red Fort. Mathur said he and the then Director of the Intelligence Bureau (IB) had briefed Modi about the security arrangements ahead of August 15.

Article Title: Midnight wasn't the end: What happened in the first few hours of Independent India
Article Text:

The beginning of a tradition

“At the stroke of the midnight hour, when the world sleeps, India will awake to life and freedom. A moment comes, which comes but rarely in history, when we step out from the old to the new, when an age ends, and when the soul of a nation, long suppressed, finds utterance. It is fitting that at this solemn moment, we take the pledge of dedication to the service of India and her people and to the still larger cause of humanity.”With those words, the first Prime Minister of Independent India, Jawaharlal Nehru , gave voice to one of the most consequential moments in the country's history.As the date changed from August 14 to August 15, 1947, nearly two centuries of British rule formally came to an end and India emerged as an independent nation.But midnight was not the culmination of the story. The first hours of freedom brought exhilaration, ceremony and celebration, but also the enormous responsibility of running a new country. A government had to begin functioning, the machinery of the state had to be inherited and reorganised, and millions of people were already caught in the upheaval of Partition.The new nation marked its freedom with flags, crowds, prayers and speeches.Yet beyond the celebrations, refugees were on the move, communal violence was spreading and India's final borders were still unknown.The story of India's freedom began before the clock struck 12. On the evening of August 14, members of the Constituent Assembly gathered in New Delhi for the historic session that would mark the transfer of power.The Assembly, which had been working on India's constitutional future, was now poised to become the central political institution of a sovereign country.Just before midnight, the chamber was charged with the knowledge that the date itself was about to change.Then came Nehru.His speech the “Tryst with Destiny”, transformed the formal transfer of power into a moment of history. He spoke of stepping “out from the old to the new”, of an age ending and the “soul of a nation” finding expression after a long period of suppression.It was the beginning.In his message to the nation published on August 15, the Prime Minister described India as “awake, vital, free and independent”, but immediately turned to the responsibilities that came with freedom. Poverty, ignorance and disease had to be fought; democratic and social institutions had to be built; and political freedom had to translate into opportunity for ordinary people.That distinction is crucial to understanding India's first day as an independent country. The midnight ceremony was not simply a celebration of Britain's departure. It was the first public act of a government that suddenly had to govern.Even before the midnight ceremony, Nehru had announced the Cabinet that would take charge from August 15. As per the announcement Nehru would handle the external affairs and commonwealth relations in addition to the Prime Minister's responsibilities. Vallabhbhai Patel took charge of home, information and broadcasting, and states. Rajendra Prasad handled food and agriculture. Maulana Abul Kalam Azad was given education. Baldev Singh took defence. B R Ambedkar was given law. R.K. Shanmukham Chetty handled finance and Rajkumari Amrit Kaur was given health, among other portfolios.The choice of August 15 was not part of the original timetable for India's independence. The British government had initially planned to transfer power by June 1948, but Lord Louis Mountbatten, the last Viceroy of British India, brought the date forward by almost a year.One reason, he later explained, was the urgency of preventing further riots, protests and bloodshed amid the worsening political and communal situation. But the date also had a personal significance for Mountbatten. August 15 was the second anniversary of Japan's surrender to the Allied powers in 1945, marking the end of the Second World War. As Supreme Allied Commander of the South-East Asia Command, Mountbatten had accepted the Japanese surrender in Singapore.Years later, in Freedom at Midnight, Mountbatten was quoted as explaining that the date had essentially “come out of the blue”. He said he wanted to demonstrate that he was in control of the transfer of power and, when pressed for a date, settled on August 15 because of its connection with Japan's surrender.But there was a problem: August 15 was considered inauspicious by astrologers consulted at the time. According to the Hindu calendar, the new day traditionally began at sunrise, making the daytime of August 15 unsuitable for such a momentous occasion.The solution was unusual but symbolic. The Constituent Assembly would meet at midnight between August 14 and August 15, allowing India to enter its new era at the precise moment the date changed in the Western calendar.That is why India's independence was ushered in not at dawn on August 15, but at the stroke of midnight.As dawn approached on August 15, the mood in Delhi shifted from solemn ceremony to public celebration. Crowds filled streets and public spaces, flags appeared everywhere and people who had spent their lives under British rule suddenly found themselves living in a country that was politically their own.The Tricolour, formally adopted by the Constituent Assembly only a few weeks earlier, became the most visible symbol of that transformation.But there was no established Independence Day script. There was no decades-old tradition of the Prime Minister appearing at the Red Fort every August 15, no familiar sequence of ceremonies for officials to repeat. India was inventing its Independence Day even as it celebrated the first one.The ceremony Indians now instinctively associate with August 15, the Prime Minister unfurling the national flag from the Red Fort, did not happen on that date in 1947.The first Independence Day was different.The Red Fort, now synonymous with India's Independence Day celebrations, was not the setting for the country's first flag-hoisting ceremony.One of the earliest known hoistings of the Tricolour in independent India took place in Madras, now Chennai, at Fort St George at 5:30 am on August 15, 1947, just hours after India formally became independent.The 12ft by 8ft pure-silk flag used for the ceremony is preserved at the Fort St George Museum and remains one of the surviving flags from that historic day. It offers a tangible link to the dawn of freedom, when the Tricolour was being raised across the country for the first time.Later that morning, Nehru hoisted the national flag at Princess Park near India Gate, rather than at the Red Fort. Historical records preserved in the Nehru Archive note that the official Independence Day function was held there.The Red Fort ceremony came the following day. Nehru unfurled the Tricolour there for the first time on August 16, 1947.That ceremony would eventually become the defining ritual of August 15, turning the Mughal-era monument into the enduring backdrop of India's annual Independence Day celebrations.There was another striking contradiction at the heart of India's first hours of freedom: Lord Louis Mountbatten, the last Viceroy of British India, did not leave with the British Raj.Instead, he became independent India's first Governor-General. The Indian Independence Act provided for the creation of two new Dominions, India and Pakistan, while Mountbatten continued in Independent India in his new constitutional role.His presence reflected the complicated nature of the transfer of power. Independence did not mean that every British institution, official or administrative arrangement disappeared at the stroke of midnight. Political authority had passed from the British Crown, but the machinery through which the subcontinent had been governed had to be repurposed almost overnight.Railways had to keep moving, communications had to be maintained, food supplies managed, finances administered, armed forces commanded, courts operated and cities policed, all while the same administrative system was being divided between India and Pakistan.Freedom, in other words, had arrived with a long to-do list.While Delhi prepared to celebrate independence with flags, speeches and crowds, Mahatma Gandhi chose to spend August 15, 1947, far from the capital, in violence-hit Calcutta.At the Constituent Assembly, his name was invoked, while outside, crowds raised cries of “Mahatma Gandhi ki jai”. But Gandhi himself was in Beliaghata, trying to prevent Hindus and Muslims from turning on each other.On August 14, Gandhi attended a packed prayer meeting and announced that he would undertake a 24-hour fast, prayer and spinning on August 15. The Gandhi Heritage Portal records that he spent Independence Day on a long fast, receiving a constant stream of visitors.Gandhi had left Delhi about two weeks earlier. After spending four days in Kashmir, he travelled to Calcutta, where communal tensions remained dangerously high.Historian Ramachandra Guha, in India After Gandhi, writes that Gandhi arrived in Calcutta on the afternoon of August 13 and took up residence in Beliaghata, at Hyderi Mansion, a building surrounded by a deeply divided neighbourhood.Gandhi deliberately chose to stay in a Muslim-owned house in a predominantly Hindu locality, accompanied by Bengal's former premier Huseyn Shaheed Suhrawardy, in an attempt to demonstrate that reconciliation was still possible.The building, now known as Gandhi Bhawan, became closely associated with one of the most extraordinary episodes surrounding Independence. Gandhi stayed there from August 13 to September 7, even as the rest of the country celebrated the end of British rule.His presence in Beliaghata was later associated with what came to be known as the “miracle of Calcutta”, after the communal violence subsided.For millions, there was no clean separation between August 15 and Partition. The creation of India and Pakistan triggered one of the largest mass migrations in modern history, as Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs who had lived for generations in the same towns and villages suddenly faced the prospect of displacement.Punjab became one of the worst centres of the violence. Lahore, a major city of undivided Punjab with a substantial Hindu and Sikh population and extensive property ownership among these communities, was caught in the upheaval.As communal tensions intensified, many had already begun leaving for Delhi and eastern Punjab, abandoning homes, businesses and belongings.Across Punjab and Bengal, the drawing of new borders turned ordinary questions of homes, farms, shops and neighbourhoods into matters of survival. Trains carrying refugees became symbols of the upheaval, with some journeys ending in massacre, while roads filled with families carrying whatever they could save.The first morning of freedom was therefore also the beginning of a traumatic displacement that would reshape the subcontinent for generations.The law came first. Independence came next.The dramatic events of August 15 can sometimes obscure the legal process that made the transfer of power possible. The Indian Independence Bill was introduced in the British House of Commons on July 4, 1947, in a remarkably low-key proceeding.A Times of India report the following day noted that the actual reading took only moments, with Prime Minister Clement Attlee rising and bowing before the Clerk read out the Bill's title.Behind that brief parliamentary ritual was legislation that would end British rule over a subcontinent of nearly 400 million people and create the two independent Dominions of India and Pakistan from August 15.The Bill provided for the partition of Punjab and Bengal, separate governments and Governor-Generals, and boundary commissions to determine territories that had yet to be finalised. It also ended British paramountcy over more than 500 princely states, with treaties and agreements between the Crown and the rulers lapsing and the states left to determine their future.Mountbatten urged the rulers to act quickly, telling them at a July 25 conference, according to The Times of India archives: “Remember that the day of transfer of power is very close at hand.” But the passage of the Act did not complete Partition. The armed forces, civil services, finances, railways, postal systems and government departments still had to be divided, while the Boundary Commissions continued their work and millions were already on the move.At the centre of this unfinished process was Sir Cyril Radcliffe, the British barrister tasked with drawing the boundaries between India and Pakistan. Having never previously travelled to India, he was given roughly five weeks to divide villages, districts, rivers, roads, canals, property and communities between the two new countries.He arrived on July 8 and worked under intense pressure, relying largely on maps and census data as communal tensions deteriorated. Radcliffe handed the Boundary Awards to Mountbatten on August 13, but they were withheld until after independence and ultimately released on August 17.India therefore celebrated its first Independence Day without knowing its complete territorial boundaries.The announcement suddenly gave places such as Lahore, Amritsar, Gurdaspur and Ferozepur new political identities, forcing families to decide whether to stay or flee. The border was not merely a line on a map but it determined who could remain in their homes and who would become a refugee.What followed was one of the largest forced migrations in history, with an estimated 20 million people uprooted from their ancestral homes. Refugees moved across the new borders as trains, roads and villages became scenes of violence, arson and death.Hundreds of thousands, and possibly close to a million people are estimated to have died in the communal carnage accompanying Partition.Andrew Mellor, in India Since Partition, records attacks on trains carrying people between the two new countries and describes widespread rioting in Punjab in the days after August 15. Killings, arson, abductions, forced conversions and attacks on entire communities turned the journey to freedom into a terrifying ordeal for millions.Years later, journalist Kuldeep Nayar recalled Radcliffe telling him that he had nearly awarded Lahore to India before deciding that Pakistan needed a major city. While the recollection cannot be independently established in every detail, it captures the extraordinary uncertainty surrounding decisions that would reshape millions of lives. For Radcliffe, the task was over. He left India on August 17 and never returned.That is what makes India's first Independence Day so different from the August 15 that Indians know today. There was no established Red Fort ceremony. There was only a country experiencing its first morning of freedom.Yet, amid all of this, something irreversible had happened.At midnight, authority had changed hands.By morning, the Tricolour was flying.The British Raj was over, and Indians were now responsible for the country they had fought to free.The first Independence Day was therefore not simply the celebration of an ending. It was the first, uncertain and extraordinary day of the much harder task that followed, building India after freedom had been won.
Article Summary: As the date changed from August 14 to August 15, 1947, India emerged as an independent nation. The first hours of freedom brought exhilaration, ceremony and celebration, but also the enormous responsibility of running a new country. The new nation marked its freedom with flags, crowds, prayers and speeches.

NEW DELHI: Bar Council of India chairman Manan Kumar Mishra on Saturday apologised to law students following the council's controversial decision to briefly halt the enrolment of National Academy of Legal Studies and Research (NALSAR) University of Law's 2026 graduating batch as advocates, Bar and Bench reported.In a letter issued on Independence Day, Mishra said he regretted any words or communication connected to the controversy that may have hurt the feelings of law students."If anything connected with the present controversy, any of my words, or letter, has hurt the feelings of our law students, I sincerely regret and apologise for the same. There should be no hesitation in saying so," the letter reads."An expression of regret is not a matter of prestige or ego. It is simply an acknowledgment that the feelings and concerns of our students matter," he added.The apology comes after the BCI directed all state bar councils not to enrol NALSAR's 2026 graduates as advocates until further orders. The council withdrew the directive within hours following an uproar on social media.The BCI had initially said it was examining allegations regarding a campaign against Chief Justice of India Surya Kant's participation in NALSAR's convocation and had sought a report identifying those responsible.The council later modified its decision to allow the enrolment of the university's 2026 graduates before withdrawing the notification altogether. The revised notification said the "vast majority" of students were innocent and should not be made to suffer for the alleged "misconduct" of a few.The controversy began after around 450 graduating NALSAR students urged the university to reconsider inviting CJI Kant as chief guest at its convocation. The students cited his alleged refusal to hear pleas concerning "police brutality" against students who had marched to Parliament on July 20 seeking the resignation of then-Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan over the NEET-UG question paper leak in May.The Supreme Court later expressed "strong disapproval" of the BCI's now-revoked order.A bench headed by CJI Kant, and comprising Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, said students have the right to protest peacefully and described the episode as a "dialogue" between him and the students."If students are protesting peacefully, who is BCI to take action? It is the right of the students to protest peacefully. It is a dialogue between students and me. No one else has to step in," the CJI said.The Supreme Court also stayed any coercive action against students or faculty by the BCI or state councils."It (the letter) was absolutely uncalled for," the bench added.
Article Summary: Bar Council of India chairman Manan Kumar Mishra apologised to law students. Mishra said he regretted any words or communication connected to the controversy that may have hurt the feelings of students. The apology comes after the BCI directed all state bar councils not to enrol NALSAR's 2026 graduates as advocates until further orders. The council withdrew the directive within hours following an uproar on social media.

Article Title: BJP says Sonia objected to full Vande Mataram; Congress says she was seeking chair for Kharge
Article Text:
Sonia Gandhi’s Vande Mataram row: BJP alleges ‘hatred’, Congress calls claim false

Congress rejects BJP's allegation

BJP escalates attack

NEW DELHI: A political row erupted on Saturday over the rendition of the full version of Vande Mataram at the Congress's Independence Day event, with the BJP accusing grand old party's former chief Sonia Gandhi of objecting to the national song and the opposition party rejecting the allegation.The BJP shared video footage from the Congress's event at Indira Bhawan and alleged that Sonia questioned party workers while Vande Mataram was being played. Congress, however, said there was no attempt to stop the full rendition and that Sonia was merely asking for a chair for party president Mallikarjun Kharge, who had been standing for some time.BJP spokesperson Gopal Krishna Agarwal, sharing the footage on X, accused the Congress of showing disrespect towards the national song. "The scene that has come to light today on Independence Day is utterly shameful."He said, "Sonia Gandhi's objection during the rendition of India's national song, 'Vande Mataram', and her questioning of Congress workers as to why it was being played exposes the Congress party's mindset."Agarwal said Vande Mataram represented more than a patriotic song, calling it a symbol of India's freedom struggle and national consciousness."Is this the same Congress that lays claim to the legacy of the nation's freedom struggle?" he asked.He also alleged that the Congress's alleged approach towards the national song reflected the party's "Emergency mindset"."The people of the country have rejected this mindset and will continue to reject it," he said.The Congress dismissed the BJP's claim and maintained that the full version of Vande Mataram was sung at its Independence Day programme.Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh cited the party's historical association with the song and referred to a 1937 meeting of the Congress Working Committee in Calcutta, attended by several prominent leaders of the freedom movement."On October 28, 1937, in Calcutta, a meeting of the Congress Working Committee was held in the presence of Mahatma Gandhi, Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, Maulana Abul Kalam Azad, Jawaharlal Nehru, Govind Ballabh Pant and C Rajagopalachari, and on the advice of Gurudev Rabindranath Tagore, they decided that the initial stanzas of Vande Mataram would be sung at the Congress sessions," Ramesh said.Ramesh said Tagore had advised Nehru and Bose that the opening portions of the song should be used at Congress gatherings."Tagore gave the advice to Nehru and Bose that the first few paragraphs of Vande Mataram should be used, he said."We have been singing those lines in every session since them, our Seva Dal sings it, our workers sing it, there is no controversy over that," Ramesh said."He stressed that the complete version was sung at Saturday's event and said the issue had already been debated extensively in Parliament."This was discussed in Parliament for 16 hours. We put forward our views. I narrated the whole history around it which the prime minister and the home minister did not know. I informed MPs of the context in which the Vande Mataram decision was taken," Ramesh said."But today, at Indira Bhawan, the full version was sung, there is no question of a controversy over it," he added.Asked specifically about the BJP's allegation that Sonia had tried to stop the full rendition, Ramesh offered a different explanation for what was seen in the video."As the Congress president was standing for a long time, Soniaji was asking for a chair for him," he said.BJP spokesperson R P Singh also targeted Sonia over the controversy, questioning her alleged opposition to the national song."Why does Antonio Maino Ji hate Vande Mataram so much? When Vande Mataram was being sung, Antonio Maino Ji reportedly became so angry that she allegedly got agitated and asked her party workers to stop it. Why such hatred for Vande Mataram?"The row over Vande Mataram comes shortly after Parliament passed legislation dealing with disrespect towards the national song. The Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Bill, 2026, was passed by the Lok Sabha through a voice vote on July 30, a day after the Rajya Sabha cleared it.The legislation grants Vande Mataram a status on par with the national anthem, Jana Gana Mana.
Article Summary: BJP accuses Congress of showing disrespect towards the national song. Opposition party says Sonia Gandhi questioned party workers while Vande Mataram was being played. Congress says there was no attempt to stop the full rendition and that Sonia was merely asking for a chair for Mallikarjun Kharge.

Article Title: 'How was leak overlooked?' Uttarakhand Congress chief demands probe into Pipalkoti tunnel tragedy
Article Text:
THDC executive director Verma said authorities had lowered the water level by around 1.5 metres and were continuously increasing the number of pumps.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Uttarakhand Pradesh Congress Committee president Ganesh Godiyal on Saturday criticised the Pushkar Singh Dhami government over the Pipalkoti tunnel accident in Chamoli district, questioning how a reported leak at the site was allegedly overlooked despite workers claiming it had persisted for some time. The criticism came as the death toll in the under-construction THDC tunnel accident rose to eight, with two workers still trapped and rescue operations continuing.Godiyal said workers injured in the accident had told him that water leakage had been occurring at the same spot for a considerable period before the tunnel was inundated by a massive surge of water."When I spoke to the injured, I learned that a leak had been occurring for quite some time at the very spot where the incident took place. How this was overlooked or why there was such apathy towards it is a matter for further investigation. NTPC provided Rs one lakh, but that amount is insufficient. I will discuss what arrangements can be made to ensure the families can sustain themselves properly," Godiyal told ANI.He also questioned the compensation announced for the families of those killed in the accident."The CM announced compensation of Rs four lakh, though I believe that amount is not sufficient," he said.Congress leader Harikrishna Bhatt echoed the criticism, saying the compensation did not reflect the value of human life and calling for safety audits across all ongoing infrastructure projects in the state."Regarding the announced compensation of Rs 4 lakh, a human life cannot be valued at merely Rs 4 lakh," Bhatt said."Safety audits should have been conducted for all such ongoing projects. The entire population of Uttarakhand is bearing the brunt of these disasters which are man-made. There is a need for a thorough analysis to determine what actual interests the people of Uttarakhand have in these large-scale projects," he added.The death toll increased to eight on Saturday after rescue teams recovered another body from the tunnel. Two other workers remain trapped inside the under-construction THDC tunnel, where operations by the National Disaster Response Force, State Disaster Response Force, District Disaster Response Force and the Indo-Tibetan Border Police are continuing.Rescue efforts have been complicated by water and accumulated sludge inside the tunnel, restricting movement and slowing the search for the remaining workers.THDC India Limited executive director Ajay Verma said the massive inflow of water appeared to have originated from a pre-existing natural cavity."Regarding the leakage and the massive influx of water in the tunnel, it appears there was a pre-existing natural cavity. During the rainy season, this cavity filled with water. The volume was so great that it found a weak point, specifically where we were excavating the tunnel from below, leading to the leakage," Verma said.He described the scale of flooding as unprecedented for a hydro-tunnel project."The inflow consists mostly of water, with very little debris. Historically, such a massive influx of water, enough to fill the tunnel for a stretch of 1.2 kilometres, is unprecedented in hydro-tunnel projects. This level of leakage is highly unusual and unexpected. It is a matter requiring investigation," he added.Verma said authorities had lowered the water level by around 1.5 metres and were continuously increasing the number of pumps."We have managed to lower the water level by about 1.5 meters. We are continuously increasing the number of pumps in operation. Running these pumps requires laying pipelines and ensuring a power supply; we are managing all these tasks simultaneously," he said.He added that less than a metre of water remained inside the tunnel."We are about to go inside with the chairman to show him how much water has been drained. Less than a metre of water remains now," Verma said."We will aim to pump out all the water by this evening and try to conclude the operation by tomorrow," he added.The accident occurred on Thursday evening when a landslide-like event near the Birhi River sent a powerful surge of water and debris into the tunnel, trapping workers who were on duty, according to NDRF team commander Amrit Lal Meena. Rescue teams are continuing efforts to pump out water, clear sludge, and reach the remaining trapped workers.
Article Summary: The death toll in the under-construction THDC tunnel accident rose to eight, with two workers still trapped and rescue operations continuing. Uttarakhand Pradesh Congress Committee president Ganesh Godiyal criticised the Pushkar Singh Dhami government over the Pipalkoti tunnel accident in Chamoli district. He questioned how a reported leak at the site was allegedly overlooked.

Article Title: 'Unfortunate, irresponsible': J&K CM Omar's Article 370, PoK remarks draw BJP fire
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: Bharatiya Janata Party on Saturday slammed Jammu and Kashmir chief minister Omar Abdullah for criticising the abrogation of Article 370 during his Independence Day speech and accused him of creating an atmosphere of confusion in the Valley.Reacting to Omar's speech, leader of opposition in Jammu and Kashmir assembly Sunil Sharma said that the abrogation of Article 370 in August 2019 strengthened the federal structure in Kashmir."The chief minister's speech was a bit regrettable. I would say this was an unfortunate and irresponsible speech because this is not a political stage. From this stage, there should be a speech for the unity, integrity and sovereignty of the country, a tribute to the soldiers, a tribute to the martyrs, and especially for the pride and honour of the Tricolour," Sharma said."I would like to tell the chief minister that it was after August 5, 2019, that this federal structure was strengthened. That is the reason why today every Kashmiri is humming Vande Mataram," the LoP said, adding that the chief minister's speech raises questions about what he wants to convey by "misusing this stage"."The whole of India accepts that Jammu and Kashmir is an integral part of them. People here are a strength, a power of this country.Not just here, but also those people across (the Line of Control) under illegal occupation. We consider them also an integral part of us, and deem them our companions," the LoP said.This comes after the chief minister, in his speech, referred to the protests in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir and said that the people on the other side of the LoC would have been protesting to rejoin India if Article 370 had not been abrogated.He said that the situation in PoK vindicates the decision of National Conference founder Sheikh Muhammad Abdullah and his colleagues to fight the Pakistan-backed tribal invaders in 1947.“When I see the situation today across the border and across the LoC, I realise that the decision taken by our leaders 80 years ago for us was the right decision,” the chief minister said. “Those who raised the slogan ‘Hamalawar Khabardar’ were right and the sacrifices they made were right,” Omar said.“Today I remember people like Master Abdul Aziz, a leader of the National Conference, who was brutally killed in Muzaffarabad (PoK) to stop those very attackers, to stop the tribals, to stop those infiltrators,” Omar said. “Today, when we see the condition of that part of Jammu and Kashmir across the LoC, we feel sad, we feel worried. For my part, I feel that perhaps if our situation had not changed in 2019, the people of that part of Jammu and Kashmir would be protesting to rejoin us today,” Omar said.“That part of Jammu and Kashmir is ours. We consider those people as our own. No one is a stranger. No one is an outsider. Even today, as per the law of Jammu and Kashmir, seats are reserved for them in the Assembly of Jammu and Kashmir, with the hope that one day those people will be able to use these vacant seats,” Omar added.
Article Summary: Omar Abdullah criticises abrogation of Article 370 during Independence Day speech. Leader of opposition in Jammu and Kashmir assembly Sunil Sharma says the speech created an atmosphere of confusion in the Valley. Omar said that the situation in PoK vindicates the decision of National Conference founder Sheikh Muhammad Abdullah to fight the Pakistan-backed tribal invaders in 1947.

NEW DELHI: Blockading NHs in Manipur by ethnic groups to inconvenience opponents is common but the Supreme Court on Friday took serious note of the humanitarian crisis such actions unleash after an NGO of Kuki women claimed that blockading of NH-2 and connected supply routes to Kangpokpi has left the population in there without food and healthcare.Senior advocate Anand Grover, appearing for Kuki Women Organisation for Human Rights, told a bench of CJI Surya Kant, and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana that the NH-2 and supply routes to Kangpokpi has been blocked by Naga groups creating a crisis for the population and requested the SC to direct the Centre and the state to reopen the NH. “The state just can’t sit and do nothing,” he complained.Intervening in the matter, an Imphal-based NGO – International Meitei Organization – through senior advocate Ngangom Junior Luwang said the Kukis had been “responsible for blocking all major NHs in Manipur since May 2023, after the Kuki-Meitei ethnic clashes began, and now they are playing the ‘victim card' when faced with the consequences of such blockades by another ethnic group.”“It is a matter of record that since May 3, 2023, members of the community, of which the petitioner is a part of, have been blocking all major NHs in Manipur - NH2 (Imphal to Dimapur), NH-37 (Imphal to Silchar), and NH-102 (Imphal to Moreh) and except for intermittent flow of goods vehicles through extortion rackets reportedly perpetuated by Kuki community,” the NGO alleged.CJI Kant said the blockade war must stop, groups must sit together, abjure violence, and cooperate with each other so that the supply of essential commodities and medicines are not disrupted.When Luwang welcomed the CJI’s suggestion, Grover immediately offered the petitioner organisation’s cooperation but wondered who would bring the Naga group to the talks.SC issued notices to the Centre, Manipur govt and National Highway Authority of India (NHAI) and said the larger public interest demands removal of blockade of all NHs in the state as well as restoration of supply to Kangpokpi district.It said Grover assured that his client in cooperation with social organisations would work towards the same and recorded similar sentiments expressed by Luwang on behalf of the Meitei NGO. It asked all the parties to suggest modalities for reopening all NHS without engaging in blame games. It posted the matter for further hearing after two weeks.
Article Summary: CJI Surya Kant said the blockade war must stop, groups must sit together, abjure violence, and cooperate with each other. An NGO of Kuki women claimed that blockading of NH-2 and connected supply routes to Kangpokpi has left the population without food and healthcare.

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday said armed Naxalism had been curbed but warned that people with Maoist thinking were still present in different parts of the country and needed to be "identified, and isolated".Addressing the nation from the ramparts of the Red Fort on the 80th Independence Day, PM Modi said the country had successfully weakened armed Naxalism but needed to remain alert against what he called "dimagi Naxals"."We need to identify these dimagi naxal, isolate them, and bring the youth together for a developed country," PM Modi said.PM Modi said Naxalism and Maoism had destroyed the aspirations of young people and kept large parts of the country under the grip of violence for decades. He also paid tribute to security personnel who lost their lives fighting the insurgency."Naxalism, Maoism destroyed the dreams of lakhs of youth. This naxalism had kept a large part of India and population as a hostage for 4 decades with the barrel of a gun, they had destroyed the Constitution," PM Modi said.He said more than 3,500 security personnel had been killed while protecting citizens from Naxal violence."More than 3,500 security personnel were martyred while protecting the people of the country. More police personnel were killed than soldiers in war, police personnel had to put their lives on the line so that people can get security. This naxalism had covered the country in blood. In 2014, when you gave us the opportunity we had decided that we will rid the country of naxalism, and today I am happy to announce that naxalism does not have even the strength for breathing," the Prime Minister added.PM Modi drew a distinction between armed Naxals and people he described as "dimagi naxal", alleging that the latter continued to look for opportunities to promote violence and push the country in what he called the wrong direction."For years, people with Maoist thinking were there in public life, even in government committees this thinking had affected various institutions and initiatives. My dear countrymen, we have been able to curb and free the country from 'hathariya naxal' (armed naxal). Even if these naxals are gone, but the 'dimagi naxal' (people with naxal thinking), are looking for an opportunity, looking to see ways of violence, and trying to drag the country to a wrong path. We need to identify these dimagi naxal, isolate them, and bring the youth together for a developed country," PM Modi said.PM Modi said areas that were once affected by Naxal violence were now witnessing development, with the Tricolour representing progress and government initiatives flying in regions where armed insurgency had previously held sway."In the 21st century, it is imperative that we eliminate the decades-old challenges that have held the country back. Naxalism and Maoism have destroyed the future of millions of young people. They have snatched away the young sons of countless mothers and shattered the dreams of families across the country. For nearly four decades, Naxalism had held large parts of India and a huge section of its population in its grip, ruling through the barrel of a gun and tearing the Constitution to shreds. More than 3,500 of our police and security personnel sacrificed their lives while protecting ordinary citizens. Naxalism had turned the land red with blood."PM Modi said the government had decided to eliminate Naxalism after coming to power in 2014 and claimed that armed Maoist violence no longer had the strength to sustain itself."When you gave us the opportunity to serve in 2014, we resolved on that very day to free the country from Naxalism.""Today, I am happy to say that Naxalite and Maoist violence no longer has the strength to sustain itself and is breathing its last. We are moving towards completely eliminating it. In areas where the bullets of Naxalites once rang out, where the soil was once stained with blood, today the same Naxal-affected regions are witnessing the tricolour of development, trust and endeavour flying high as they move towards becoming Naxalism-free. "During his Independence Day address, PM Modi also referred to challenges India faced over the past several years, including the Covid-19 pandemic and conflicts in Ukraine and West Asia."In the last 20-12 years, we have faced many dangers. As soon as we emerged from Covid, there was news of wars that started to arise from Ukraine side and West Asia. An atmosphere of tension prevailed. God knows what all the predictions the predictors made!," he said.PM Modi said attempts were also made to create fear among citizens through rumours over the availability of vaccines, petrol, diesel and fertilisers.The remarks formed part of PM Modi's wider Independence Day address, in which he outlined the government's priorities and India's development ambitions as the country moves towards the goal of becoming a developed nation by 2047.

NEW DELHI: The United Nations Security Council (UNSC) has officially attributed the November 2025 blast near Delhi’s iconic Red Fort to Al-Qaida in the Indian Subcontinent (AQIS), according to the 38th report of its Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team.The attack on November 10 last year claimed 11 lives."Al-Qaida in the Indian Subcontinent (AQIS, not listed) continued to evolve from a fragmented group into a regional terrorist entity; it established logistics and financial networks, working in decentralised, small, scattered cells instead of large units. The attack in November 2025 on the Red Fort in Delhi was officially attributed to AQIS," the report, published on August 10, stated.The assessment marks a significant shift in the attribution of the Red Fort attack, which had earlier been linked to the Pakistan-based Jaish-e-Mohammed (JeM).The report noted that one member state had attributed a series of attacks to JeM and also linked the group to the Red Fort blast.The explosion occurred around 7 pm when a moving Hyundai i20 erupted in flames near the iconic monument.Investigators identified Umar-e-Nabi as the driver of the car and suspect him of carrying out the attack as a suicide bomber.Read also: Red Fort blast: 7,500-page NIA charge sheet alleges ‘Operation Heavenly Hind’ to overthrow govt Launched in 2014, AQIS is a regional affiliate of Al-Qaida.The group was formed to expand the organisation’s activities across South Asia, including India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and parts of Afghanistan.Meanwhile, the latest UNSC assessment also flagged broader concerns over the activities and capabilities of Al-Qaida and Islamic State (ISIL/Da’esh) affiliates.The report noted that Al-Qaida and ISIL had for years shown interest in developing chemical and biological weapons but had so far failed to overcome the technical challenges involved. It also highlighted the widespread circulation of instructions on producing such agents in online terrorist communities.The report cited material published by ISIL’s English-language Invade magazine in February that included instructions related to botulinum toxin and cyanide. It also noted that ISIL-K had shown particular interest in ricin and circulated instructions on developing the toxin over the previous 12 months.
